text: Our world went upside down here a year or so ago, so we're still trying to get out of it. Starting April 5th, anyone age 60 or older in Michigan that wishes to be vaccinated will be eligible. And I think not only is the Johnson & Johnson vaccine getting ready to be added on, but I heard on the news tonight that the AstraZeneca may be approved here very shortly. So the more vaccines are available, the faster this process can go. And it really is going really well now. So I think once we get to a point that we've got the vast majority of people vaccinated, then I think we're going to start seeing the numbers starting to go down a little bit. But finally, as far as COVID issues, if you or any of your constituents are being stymied by the Unemployment Insurance Agency, we have been fairly successful in making contact with them for our constituents. So have your constituents or yourself reach out and contact my office at jimallison at house.mi.gov or at 517-373-3818. I've got a staffer that's kind of dedicated to that and she's been pretty successful. So we've been able to cut some red tape, even with no scissors. So a couple of things coming up on the legislation goals. This is something that I think Mayor Grassley knew was coming. This week I'm going to be introducing a bill to name a section of I-75 between 12 Mile and 14 Mile Road in honor of our recently passed Fire Captain Jeffrey Brozek. That bill is written and will probably be dropped tomorrow or Wednesday and we'll follow that and get that approved. And then they'll put signs up and it'll say this highway is in honor of Captain. So that's kind of fun. We had a meeting this morning. We have told some of you that we formed an Oakland County Democratic Caucus with our Oakland County legislators, our representatives, and our Senate. And we did that so we can take advantage of the fact that we've got Democratic leadership at the county level so that we can work closely together and coordinate efforts at the State House and the State Senate with needs that the county executives have. It's an opportunity we haven't had before so we're going to take advantage of it. Also, I'm serving as chairman of that one, of that caucus, but I'm also vice chair of the house of the, where'd I go here, of the Municipal Leadership Caucus that's being put together by MML to focus on statewide municipal finance. Municipal finance is one of the key things. It's my top initiative this year. I did drop a bill last year dealing with modifications to the Headley Amendment, which didn't go anywhere, but we're going to revamp that bill. Basically what it does, when Headley was passed back in 1978, some of you may remember, some of you may not be aware, that not only did it have a roll-down provision, which we're living with now, but it also had a roll-up provision that would allow you to roll your tax rate back up when the economy got better so you take advantage of your increased value. But when Prop A was passed in 1994, that provision was eliminated. So right now what Headley allows you to do is roll your tax rate down, but you can't roll it back up even if the economy improves without going through the formula of 5% of the rate of inflation, whichever is less. So we're working on that as long as some other ideas dealing with state-shared revenue try to get more guaranteed and fair system for state-shared revenue. What else have I got here? Oh, I did introduce a bill early on this year. My first bill dealt with remediation of contaminated sites like we've got over on 696. What my bill does is it eliminates the statute of limitations on bad actors. Right now the law, if so many years expire, you can't go all the way back to the owner of the property that may have caused the pollution and you're stuck with dealing with the person that happened to move in and didn't know about it. It really doesn't have any effect on our situation we're dealing with right now with the Chromium place, but it will help in the future. And there's also a companion bill that was sponsored by my colleague, Usain Robbie, that defines what the fines are for that. So it's just cleaning up some ambiguous language and helping us enforce the law and get these bad guys to pay their bills. Also dropped a bill as part of a bipartisan aid bill, elder abuse package, which is a number of bills that will clean up legislation and definitions of who is an elder and how do they qualify. And the bill I dropped in this package was dealing with penalties for someone who tries to fraudulently take money from an elderly person or from their mother, father, aunt, uncle, whoever they're dealing with. And it just defines that. The rest of them deal with penalties and licensing and various things dealing with the elderly. I guess what I'm saying is we're finally getting back and getting legislation passed rather than just trying to dole out the state's money that they're trying to give us, the federal money they're trying to give us. You're probably all aware of the Federal American Rescue Act, which just came out last week. Still trying to define what's in it. We know that the basic package is $1.9 trillion, $350 billion nationally is going to go to state and local governments. How that dollar amount is going to be divided is still being determined. We've heard some ideas of what's going to happen, but until we get into what it really is, the amounts and how it's going to be split up and what you can spend it on and what you can't spend it on, we just know it's coming. We just don't know how much. That being said, everybody I talk to, I advise. My dad used to tell me this, don't let that money burn a hole in your pocket. When you get that money, if you've got time to use it, make sure you can leverage it to get more out of your money. You can use it probably to do an infrastructure project that maybe you've been putting off because there hasn't been money. Before you just start promising that money, I know people are already coming up and saying, use it for this, use it for that. Just do your homework and try to invest money where it's going to affect the city in the most positive way. The other problem we've got is we've been fighting a battle with the distribution of the federal money, federal and state money. There's a stalemate between the Republican side of the House and the Democratic side of the House, where being a minority, the Democrats don't have a whole lot to say about what goes in, but the Republicans wrote the bills and allocating some money for schools and cities and other entities. They didn't use all of the money that was available. Our concern, number one, is that if they don't use it by September, it's going to go away. We're hoping to get all the money allocated, even if it's not going to be spent, just have it dedicated. The other more troubling part of it is they've tie-barred this to a legislative bill that would require the governor to cede some of her responsibilities, as well as Health and Human Services cede their responsibilities back to the legislature so that they can have control. They're basically trying to get the governor to give up her role as the executive of the state in order to get this money. In other words, they're holding it hostage for us. They're looking for ransom demands and that kind of stuff. The bills were submitted, the bills were passed, and she vetoed. She line-item vetoed them. They came back and Republicans tried to get a veto override, which requires two-thirds votes of the House, and they couldn't get it. We're still sitting there. The money is not allocated yet. The governor and the House Appropriations Chairman were supposed to be sitting down and discussing how we're going to allocate this money, but we get into personality issues. If anybody's following the news, it's pretty obvious that the Republicans right now are pretty angry with the governor. It's not a good environment to get stuff done, but we continue to try to get it done. The money will get out. It's just how much and when. We're working on that.
